questions.q: In a classic predator-prey relationship, why does the predator population peak shortly after the prey population peaks?
options: Predators cause prey numbers to rise
Predators reproduce before prey are available
Prey numbers never affect predator numbers
Abundant prey allows more predators to survive and reproduce, with a time lag
questions.explain: A peak in prey provides plentiful food, so predator numbers rise afterwards, lagging behind the prey peak.

questions.q: How does secondary succession differ from primary succession?
options: It involves no change in species over time
It begins on land that already has soil, e.g. after a fire
It begins on bare rock with no soil
It never reaches a climax community
questions.explain: Secondary succession starts where soil already exists, so it proceeds faster than primary succession.

questions.q: What is the role of saprobiotic (decomposer) bacteria and fungi in ammonification?
options: They fix atmospheric nitrogen
They release nitrogen gas from nitrate
They oxidise nitrite to nitrate
They convert nitrogen-containing compounds in dead matter into ammonium ions
questions.explain: Decomposers break down proteins and other nitrogen compounds in dead organisms, releasing ammonium ions.

questions.q: Natural selection leads to evolution because:
options: Alleles that increase survival and reproduction become more frequent over generations
Mutations are always beneficial
Individuals change their genes during their lifetime to suit the environment
All individuals reproduce equally
questions.explain: Differential survival and reproduction of advantageous alleles increases their frequency in the gene pool over time.

A small group establishes a new population carrying only a subset of the original gene pool
A large population is split equally by a barrier
Selection favours heterozygotes
questions.explain: A few founding individuals carry only part of the parent population's genetic variation, skewing allele frequencies in the new population.

questions.q: Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are reproductively isolated by:
options: A change in mating season only
Polyploidy
A geographical barrier such as a mountain or river
A behavioural difference within the same area
questions.explain: In allopatric speciation a physical/geographical barrier separates populations, allowing them to diverge.

questions.q: The maximum population size an environment can support sustainably is known as the:
options: Carrying capacity
Limiting factor
Climax population
Biotic potential
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population an ecosystem's resources can support over a long period.

Which sampling technique is most appropriate for estimating the population of a non-motile plant such as clover in a field?
options: Sweep netting
Pitfall traps
Mark-release-recapture
Quadrats placed at random
questions.explain: Random quadrats are ideal for sessile organisms like plants, where individuals can be counted in a known area.

questions.q: A high value of an index of diversity (e.g. Simpson's index) for a habitat indicates:
options: A single dominant species
Many species each fairly evenly represented
Few species and many individuals of one species
Low resistance to environmental change
questions.explain: A high diversity index reflects many species in relatively even proportions, indicating a more stable ecosystem.

questions.q: Which of the following is a prezygotic reproductive isolating mechanism?
options: Hybrid sterility
Death of the hybrid embryo
Differences in courtship behaviour preventing mating
Hybrid breakdown in later generations
questions.explain: Behavioural (courtship) isolation prevents mating, acting before a zygote can form, so it is prezygotic.
